\section[\texorpdfstring{\sk{पृथिवी} (pṛthivī)}{पृथिवी (pṛthivī)}]{\sk{पृथिवी} (pṛthivī) — the earth}

\label{lesson:SA-C251-prthivi}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Sanskrit for a building, then the Sanskrit for lodging.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{पृथिवी}}
\textbf{\sk{पृथिवी}} — \emph{pṛthivī} — \textquotedblleft{}the earth\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{pṛthivī} is the feminine of \emph{pṛthu}, \textquotedblleft{}broad, wide\textquotedblright{} (MW): the earth is \textquotedblleft{}the broad, extended one\textquotedblright{}. MW compares \emph{pṛthu} with Greek \emph{platys}, \textquotedblleft{}broad\textquotedblright{}, and English \emph{plate}, so the word is inherited from Indo-European.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for this chapter.
\end{grammarlens}

  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{pṛthivī}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} say \emph{pṛthivī}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Sanskrit for a building, then the Sanskrit for lodging, then say \emph{pṛthivī} again
\end{itemize}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\sk{जगत्} (jagat)}{जगत् (jagat)}]{\sk{जगत्} (jagat) — the universe, the world}

\label{lesson:SA-C251-jagat}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Sanskrit for lodging, then the Sanskrit for the earth.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{जगत्}}
\textbf{\sk{जगत्}} — \emph{jagat} — \textquotedblleft{}the universe, the world\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{jagat} is a reduplicated form of the root √gam, \textquotedblleft{}to go\textquotedblright{} (MW): \textquotedblleft{}moving, living\textquotedblright{}. In the Rigveda it means \textquotedblleft{}men and animals\textquotedblright{}, and in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa \textquotedblleft{}the world\textquotedblright{} (CDIAL 5078): the world as everything that moves.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for this chapter.
\end{grammarlens}

  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{jagat}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} say \emph{jagat}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Sanskrit for lodging, then the Sanskrit for the earth, then say \emph{jagat} again
\end{itemize}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\sk{लोकः} (lokaḥ)}{लोकः (lokaḥ)}]{\sk{लोकः} (lokaḥ) — the world, people}

\label{lesson:SA-C251-lokah}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Sanskrit for the earth, then the Sanskrit for the universe.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{लोकः}}
\textbf{\sk{लोकः}} — \emph{lokaḥ} — \textquotedblleft{}the world, people\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{loka} is a Rigvedic word for \textquotedblleft{}free space, the world\textquotedblright{}, and later \textquotedblleft{}people\textquotedblright{} (CDIAL 11119). MW compares Latin \emph{lūcus}, first \textquotedblleft{}a clearing in a forest\textquotedblright{}. Hindi \emph{loī}, \textquotedblleft{}people\textquotedblright{}, comes from it.
\end{cousinweb}

\end{grammarlens}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\sk{प्रकृतिः} (prakṛtiḥ)}{प्रकृतिः (prakṛtiḥ)}]{\sk{प्रकृतिः} (prakṛtiḥ) — nature}

\label{lesson:SA-C251-prakrtih}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Sanskrit for the universe, then the Sanskrit for the world.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{प्रकृतिः}}
\textbf{\sk{प्रकृतिः}} — \emph{prakṛtiḥ} — \textquotedblleft{}nature\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{prakṛti} is built on \emph{pra}, \textquotedblleft{}before, forth\textquotedblright{}, and the root √kṛ, \textquotedblleft{}to make\textquotedblright{} (MW): \textquotedblleft{}making or placing first\textquotedblright{}, and so the original or natural form of anything. From there it came to mean \textquotedblleft{}nature\textquotedblright{} (CDIAL 8446).
\end{cousinweb}

\end{grammarlens}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\sk{पंकः} (paṅkaḥ)}{पंकः (paṅkaḥ)}]{\sk{पंकः} (paṅkaḥ) — mud}

\label{lesson:SA-C251-pankah}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Sanskrit for the world, then the Sanskrit for nature.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{पंकः}}
\textbf{\sk{पंकः}} — \emph{paṅkaḥ} — \textquotedblleft{}mud\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{paṅka} is mud or mire (MW), and MW reports that it is said to come from a root √pac, \textquotedblleft{}to spread\textquotedblright{}, so its origin is uncertain. It lives on as Hindi \emph{paṅkā}, \textquotedblleft{}mud\textquotedblright{}, and the lotus is \emph{paṅkaja}, \textquotedblleft{}mud-born\textquotedblright{} (CDIAL 7645).
\end{cousinweb}

One more word for this chapter.
\end{grammarlens}
